latin.347: LUTHERANORUM famosior propositionis interpretatio duplex est. Altera Lutheri: Hoc, seu hic panis, est corpus meum, i. e. in, cum & sub hoc pane est corpus meum, Tom. II. Witteberg. sermone contra Fanaticos pag. 98. Laß sie / die Schwärmer / (ita suo more cognominat eos quos non habet in controversia sacramentaria ὁμοψήφους) fabren / und laß uns bey den Worten bleiben wie sie lauten: Daß IM BROD der Leib Christi und IM WEIN warhafftig sein Blut sey.
latin.348: Altera Flacii Illyrici: Hoc complexum, seu haec massa ex duabus rebus constans, est corpus meum; quorum utraque apertissimè tropica; prior metonymica, Continentis pro contento, posterior synechdochica, Partis pro toto.
latin.349: Neque est, quod in gratiam posterioris, ceu famosissimae hodieque magis receptae, vel pro hujus proprietate, Sebast. Schmidius excipiat: τὸ Hoc, complexum denotans, cùm simul sit demonstrativum, prohibere, quò minus propositio tropica evadat.
latin.350: Nam respondeo (1) Complexum nondum probatum esse, (2) Complexum Luthero improbari, per pronomen hoc nihil aliud quam panem intelligendum edicenti, tùm in libro contra Regem Angliae, ubi ait: Ex filo sermonis ostendi, pronomen hoc ad panem aptari & sic sonare aperta verba: Hoc est corpus meum i. e. hic panis est corpus meum: Nam Textus sic habet: accepit panem &c. vides hic quòd omnia illa verba: accepit, benedixit, fregit &c. de pane dicantur, & eundem demonstrat pronomen hoc, quia id ipsum quod benedixit, fregit & dedit, hoc inquam acceptum benedictum & fractum significatur, cum dicitur: hoc est corpus meum. Non praedicatum, sed subjectum demonstratur. Non enim corpus suum accepit, benedixit & fregit, sed panem. &c. hae sunt clara verba quae Rex nequitiosus occulit & nudam illam propositionem urget: Hoc est corpus meum, & pronomen hoc ad corpus propriè & immediatè aptat.
latin.351: Tum in Libro de captivitate Babylonica, Credo inquit, firmiter non modo corpus Christi esse in pane, sed panem esse corpus Christi. Sic enim me servabunt Verba, ubi dicit: accepit panem, gratias agens fregit & dixit: accipite, manducate. Hoc, i. e. hic panis, quem acceperat & fregerat, est corpus meum. Et Paulus, nonne panis quem frangimus participatio corporis Christi est? non dicit (NB.) in pane est; sed ipse panis est participatio corporis Christi, & paulò post ipse usus loquendi & sensus communis probat subjectum sic monstrativum panis (NB.) dum dicit, hoc est corpus meum.
latin.352: (3.) Positô, non concessô Complexô, partem sic praedicari de toto, & propositionem tropicam fieri. (4.) Demonstrationem non tollere complexum, Ergo nec tropum. (5.) Demonstrationem tantum ad illud pertinere, quod demonstrari sensibus poterat; & hoc vel erat corpus Christi, mensae assidens: sic verò propositionem enasci Carlstadianam, vel panis, quem in manibus gestabat Christus: sic verò nostram obtenturam metonymiam signi pro signato; vel denique aliud invisibile corpus Christi: sed hoc primò non poterat sensui demonstrari, quia ex hypothesi invisibile est; dein duo corpora Christi inducit, aliud visibile, aliud invisibile, praeterquàm quòd tertiò alterutrum corpus unà cum pane acceptum, tam Complexum, nondum probatum, quin Luthero improbatum, quàm proprietatem, magno molimine impugnatam, aegreque concedendam, reducem facit.

pass_a.347: The more famous Lutheran interpretation of the proposition is twofold. One is Luther’s: This, or this bread, is my body — i.e. in, with, and under this bread is my body (Wittenberg Tom. II, sermon against the Fanatics, p. 98). Let them / the Schwärmer / (so he is used to nickname those with whom he is not ὁμοψῆφος in the sacramentarian controversy) fabren / and let us remain by the words as they sound: That IN THE BREAD the body of Christ and IN THE WINE His blood truly is.
pass_a.348: The other is Flacius Illyricus’s: This complex, or this mass consisting of two things, is my body; of which both [readings] are most openly tropical — the former metonymic, of Container for contained; the latter synecdochic, of Part for whole.
pass_a.349: Nor is it that Sebastian Schmidius should except in favor of the latter — as the most famous and today more received — or for its propriety: that τὸ Hoc, denoting a complex and at the same time being demonstrative, should forbid the proposition from turning out tropical.
pass_a.350: For I reply (1) that the Complex has not yet been proved, (2) that the Complex is disapproved by Luther, who lays down that by the pronoun this nothing other than bread is to be understood — then in the book against the King of England, where he says: From the thread of the speech I have shown that the pronoun this is fitted to the bread and so the open words sound: This is my body i.e. this bread is my body: For the Text so has: he took bread &c. You see here that all those words — he took, blessed, broke &c. — are said of the bread, and the same the pronoun this demonstrates, because that very thing which He blessed, broke and gave — this, I say, received, blessed and broken — is signified when it is said: this is my body. Not the predicate but the subject is demonstrated. For He did not take, bless and break His body, but bread. &c. These are clear words which the wicked King hid and presses that naked proposition This is my body, and fits the pronoun this properly and immediately to the body.
pass_a.351: Then in the Book on the Babylonian Captivity: I believe, he says, firmly not only that Christ’s body is in the bread, but that the bread is Christ’s body. For so the Words will keep me, where He says: He took bread, giving thanks broke and said: take, eat. This, i.e. this bread which He had taken and broken, is my body. And Paul: is not the bread which we break a participation of the body of Christ? He does not say (NB.) it is in the bread; but the bread itself is a participation of Christ’s body, and a little later the very usage of speech and common sense proves the subject thus demonstrative of bread (NB.) when He says, this is my body.
pass_a.352: (3.) The Complex being put, not conceded, a part is thus predicated of the whole, and the proposition becomes tropical. (4.) Demonstration does not remove the complex, therefore neither the trope. (5.) Demonstration pertains only to that which could be demonstrated to the senses; and this was either Christ’s body sitting at the table — thus a Carlstadian proposition would arise — or the bread which Christ was carrying in His hands — thus our metonymy of sign for thing signified would obtain — or finally another invisible body of Christ: but this first could not be demonstrated to sense, because by hypothesis it is invisible; then it introduces two bodies of Christ, one visible, one invisible — besides that thirdly either body received together with the bread makes both the Complex (not yet proved, nay disapproved by Luther) and propriety (assaulted with great effort and hardly to be conceded) return.

347: The better-known Lutheran reading of This is my body is twofold.
Luther’s: This / this bread is my body means in, with, and under this bread is my body (Wittenberg Tom. II vs the Fanatics, p. 98).
Let the Schwärmer go — his nickname for those not ὁμοψῆφος with him on the sacrament — and stay with the words as they sound: IN THE BREAD Christ’s body, IN THE WINE His blood truly.
348: Flacius Illyricus’s other reading: This complex / this mass of two things is my body.
Both readings are openly tropical — Luther’s as metonymy of container for contained; Flacius’s as synecdoche of part for whole.
349: Sebastian Schmidius tries to save Flacius’s more famous reading (or its propriety): τὸ Hoc names a complex and is demonstrative at once, so the proposition cannot turn tropical.
Strimesius will not let that exception stand.
350: Reply (1): the Complex is not yet proved.
Reply (2): Luther himself rejects it — hoc means nothing but bread.

Against the King of England he threads the Institution verbs (took, blessed, broke) onto the bread: This is my body = this bread is my body; the pronoun shows the subject, not the predicate — the King hid those clear words and pressed the naked proposition onto the body.
351: In On the Babylonian Captivity Luther believes not only that Christ’s body is in the bread, but that the bread is Christ’s body — the Words keep him: This = this bread He took and broke.

Paul likewise: the bread we break is participation of Christ’s body — he does not say (NB.) it is in the bread, but the bread itself is that participation; common speech proves the demonstrative subject is bread when He says this is my body.
352: (3.) Grant the Complex only for argument: then a part is predicated of the whole, and the proposition is tropical.
(4.) A demonstrative does not cancel the complex — therefore not the trope either.

(5.) Sense can only point to what senses reach: the sitting body (Carlstadt), the bread in Christ’s hands (Reformed sign-for-signified metonymy), or an invisible second body — which cannot be shown to sense, doubles Christ’s bodies, and drags back both the unproved Complex Luther rejected and a propriety hardly to be conceded.

notes.352: Replies (3)–(5); Carlstadt vs metonymy; stop before §.V.
